claims.text: The balance between bulk configurational entropy and surface/interface energetic contributions governs the high-temperature structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys.
Decreasing nanoparticle size increases the surface-to-volume ratio.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio makes surface energetic effects more dominant.
Smaller high-entropy-alloy particles have enhanced nanoscale lattice strain.
Size-enhanced surface energetic and lattice-strain effects destabilize the ordered phase.
Increasing the relative contribution of surface/interface energy over bulk configurational entropy lowers the barrier to oxidation.
Increasing the relative contribution of surface/interface energy over bulk configurational entropy lowers the barrier to phase separation.
In smaller nanoparticles, destabilizing surface effects outweigh stabilization from the disordered bulk.
Smaller nanoparticles will oxidize faster than larger particles of the same composition and processing history at high temperature.
Smaller nanoparticles will undergo more rapid phase decomposition than larger particles.
Smaller nanoparticles will develop a higher degree of structural disorder than larger particles.
Larger nanoparticles will retain better phase integrity under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
The predicted size dependence applies approximately from 800 to 1000 °C for exposures up to about 100 hours in controlled oxidizing environments.
Impurities or extreme environmental conditions may override surface/interface effects.
The quantitative size dependence of degradation may depend on particle morphology.
The quantitative size dependence of degradation may depend on protective-oxide formation.
